The same empirical shortening factor k is used for the monopole and both dipole arms. Use 0.95 as a starting point and measure the antenna after installation. Choose k and the cable velocity factor VF independently.
A low k does not account for coils or loading: this model is intended for straight conductors.
Ideal λ/4 — monopole and each arm
This is five eighths of the free-space wavelength. A practical 5/8-wave vertical typically needs a matching network and a suitable conductive ground plane or radials.

The dipole has two equal arms. Their combined length excludes the feed-point gap. The monopole length covers the radiator only; radials are not included. The radials or a conductive ground plane form the other part of the antenna and provide a return path for radio-frequency current. Their dimensions and arrangement affect tuning and must be chosen separately.
Use these dimensions as a starting point. Conductor diameter, insulation, mounting and nearby objects all affect the resonant length. Measure the antenna and adjust its length as needed.

Treat the result as an estimate. Change the length in small steps in the final installation and measure again after each step. When trimming, start by removing only part of the estimated length change.
Adjust both arms by the same amount. The calculator shows the total length change and the change to each arm separately.
Large adjustment: the simple ratio may be inaccurate. Check the construction and measure again.
The result is outside the supported input length range; check whether the model applies. The result has not been clamped.
Enter valid values to see the result.
Enter the actual length of the antenna you built. A theoretical length is not substituted here.
Enter a positive number with a decimal point or comma, without signs or spaces within the number
The value must be greater than zero
The factor must be greater than 0 and no greater than 1
No more than four significant decimal places
Lₛ is the vertical radiator length from the feed point to the tip. Choose the radials separately.
Lₐ is the length of each equal dipole arm. Total length Lᵈ equals 2Lₐ and excludes the feed gap.
Use frequency f in hertz (Hz) to obtain wavelength λ in metres (m). The speed of light in vacuum is c = 299 792 458 m/s.

L₀ is the actual length and L₁ is the estimated length after tuning. fₘ is the measured resonant frequency and fₜ is the target. The estimate assumes the same resonant mode and essentially the same construction. It is less accurate for antennas with loading coils, traps or complex geometry.
Wavelength equals the speed of light divided by frequency.
The monopole length is one quarter of the wavelength multiplied by the shortening factor k.
The total dipole length is half the wavelength multiplied by k. Each arm is half the total dipole length.
The length is five eighths of the wavelength.
The new length equals the actual length multiplied by the measured resonant frequency and divided by the target frequency.
The length change is the new length minus the actual length.
Each new arm length is half the new total dipole length. The adjustment to each arm is half the total length change.
Lₛ is the monopole length, Ld the total dipole length and La the length of one arm. The shortening factor k applies to the conductor length, not the wavelength. Choose k to suit the antenna design.
A negative ΔL predicts a decrease in length and a positive ΔL predicts an increase. Equal frequencies give zero change.

Enter the frequency where input reactance X is close to zero. If you only measure SWR, use the frequency of its minimum as an approximation.

The entered length differs by more than 25% from the starting estimate for this antenna type at the measured frequency and k = 0.95. Check the antenna type, length units and resonant mode before changing the length. This is a guide for checking the model.
Measure impedance in the final installation. With a VNA, set the reference plane at the feed point or compensate for the measurement cable.
When the measured resonant frequency fₘ is below the target fₜ, reducing the length usually moves resonance up.
When the measured resonant frequency fₘ is above the target fₜ, increasing the length usually moves resonance down.

Illustrative SWR curve without a numerical scale. The example places the minimum near fₘ. In a real antenna, the SWR minimum can occur at a different frequency from the point where X is close to zero.
